speaker: Oriol Vinyals
title: No Priors Ep. 74 | With Google DeepMind VP of Research Oriol Vinyals
question: In frontier AI training, what determines how compute is split across pretraining, reinforcement learning, and inference-time search?
guest: Historically, if you look at AlphaGo, which followed the recipe of training on human data, using RL to make it better, and doing search at inference time, the majority of compute was spent on the reinforcement learning self-play loop. Today that's clearly not the case. Most compute is spent in training, and in fact, you have to stop the reinforcement learning process so you don't overfit to imperfect reward functions. Otherwise, you start doing adversarial search against a reward function based on human preferences—all of a sudden, the model discovers you can issue lots of emoticons and the reward function thinks that's great. Clearly, reward functions aren't as accurate as in Go or chess. So going forward, training might be around fifty percent rather than over ninety like today, and the rest mostly on reinforcement learning once we get access to good rewards. For inference time, unless you ask the model to solve protein folding where you can wait a month, a few seconds of compute is okay, so that's a small percentage compared to training.

points.core: Better reward functions shift a much larger compute share into reinforcement learning.
points.note: Accept: pretraining share dropping from over 90% toward roughly half as reliable rewards unlock large-scale RL self-improvement like AlphaGo. Do not credit: claiming pretraining will always consume virtually all compute.

points.core: Per-query inference search remains smaller than training compute for interactive tasks.
points.note: Accept: latency constraints keeping test-time compute to seconds for normal queries, with massive inference budgets reserved for offline scientific problems. Do not credit: claiming test-time search eliminates the need for large training compute.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
No fixed rule sets the split; it is an economic optimization where labs push each marginal unit of compute toward whatever buys the most capability or revenue per dollar, subject to practical constraints.

The main drivers are these. First, marginal returns: pretraining scales predictably but with diminishing (roughly log-linear) gains, so as it saturates, RL and post-training on reasoning tasks become more attractive, provided good environments and reward signals exist. Second, amortization: training compute is a one-time cost spread across every future query, while inference-time search (longer reasoning, sampling, verification) is paid per use. High-volume, easy tasks therefore favor investing in training; rare, high-value, hard tasks favor spending at inference. Third, substitutability: training and test-time compute trade off against each other (as shown in AlphaGo-style systems, where more search can replace much more training), so the exchange rate between them matters. Fourth, practical limits: data availability, the supply of verifiable RL tasks, latency tolerance, hardware supply, serving demand, and how much compute goes to experiments rather than final runs.

In practice, the split is set empirically and shifts with each generation.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: In frontier AI, compute allocation across pretraining, reinforcement learning, and inference-time search is governed by marginal scaling returns, data availability, task verifiability, and deployment economics. Pretraining builds broad world knowledge and representations, absorbing massive upfront compute until high-quality human data grows scarce and parameter scaling hits diminishing returns. Once a base model is capable enough to occasionally sample viable solutions, compute shifts toward reinforcement learning. Because RL scores synthetic rollouts against programmatic verifiers or reward models in domains like math, coding, and agentic tool use, labs scale it past human-data bottlenecks until exploration plateaus or reward hacking arises. Balancing training against inference-time search then comes down to amortization, query volume, and latency budgets. Pretraining and RL are fixed upfront investments amortized across all future requests, whereas test-time search incurs per-query cost and delay. Labs therefore distill successful search traces back into model weights for high-volume, low-latency traffic, reserving heavy inference-time search for hard, high-stakes queries where accuracy outweighs cost and speed.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
There's no fixed formula. Labs set the split empirically by asking where the next unit of compute buys the most capability, given what they expect deployment to cost.

The main factor is marginal return per FLOP at each stage, measured with scaling-law experiments. Pretraining gains shrink as compute grows and as good data runs out. RL on verifiable tasks like math, code and agentic work has recently delivered steep gains, which is why RL's share has grown sharply. xAI, for example, said Grok 4 used RL compute on the scale of its pretraining. The stages also depend on each other: RL and search mostly amplify what a strong base model can already do, so skimping on pretraining limits both.

Economics matters just as much. Training is a one-time cost, but inference cost grows with every user and query. High-volume products push labs to "overtrain" smaller models, going beyond Chinchilla-optimal ratios to make serving cheaper. Test-time search makes the most sense for rare, high-value queries where latency is acceptable. Snell et al. (2024) found that extra inference compute can substitute for pretraining on easy and medium problems but not on hard ones.

Other factors include the hardware available, how many good RL environments exist, and competitive pressure. The actual splits labs use are mostly not public.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: In frontier AI development, the compute split across pretraining, reinforcement learning, and inference-time search is governed primarily by marginal capability gains per FLOP, task verifiability, and deployment economics. Pretraining receives the foundational share because it builds broad world knowledge and general representations, though its allocation is increasingly constrained by high-quality data ceilings and diminishing returns on complex reasoning. Reinforcement learning claims a growing portion of training compute whenever reliable, scalable reward signals or verifiers exist—such as in mathematics, coding, and agentic tool use—where it elicits reasoning and problem-solving behaviors far more compute-efficiently than further pretraining. Finally, balancing upfront training against inference-time search hinges on amortization and latency budgets. Because pretraining and reinforcement learning are fixed costs spread across billions of queries, labs favor them for high-volume, latency-sensitive applications. Conversely, for harder, lower-volume, or high-value problems, shifting compute into test-time search yields steeper accuracy gains per dollar than simply training a larger base model.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
The split depends on how much each additional unit of compute improves performance on the tasks the model will actually face. Pretraining builds broad capabilities that can be reused across every request. Reinforcement learning can make desired behaviors more reliable, especially when training tasks have rewards or outcomes that are cheap and reliable to verify. Inference-time search spends compute on individual requests, where generating and checking more candidate answers can help on difficult problems.

Teams estimate those returns by varying compute at each stage and measuring quality, cost, and latency. The stages also interact. A stronger pretrained model may produce better candidates for reinforcement learning and search, while reinforcement learning may teach the model to solve problems with fewer attempts. Upfront training costs can be spread across many requests, whereas search costs recur each time it is used. High request volume and tight latency budgets therefore favor improvements learned during training, while occasional hard, high-value problems can justify more search at inference. There is no universal ratio.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
There’s no universal split. Teams allocate compute according to which use delivers the largest expected gain on their target tasks for the cost. Pretraining builds broad capabilities, and its return depends partly on the quality and quantity of available data. Reinforcement learning is especially useful when a reliable reward signal can steer the model toward better answers. Inference-time search spends extra compute on a particular problem, for example by generating several solutions and checking which one works. Its value depends on the difficulty of the problem and how reliably the system can recognize a good solution.

Deployment volume and latency matter because training costs are paid up front, while search costs recur on each query. A frequently used model may justify more training to make each answer cheaper or faster. For a rare, difficult query, extra search may be the better investment. Teams estimate these tradeoffs through experiments at different compute budgets, accounting for interactions such as reinforcement learning making search more effective.
